text: We like to think. <break time="0.8s" /> That breakthroughs in research. <break time="0.8s" /> Are the result of a simple process of gathering evidence. <break time="0.8s" /> From which we then draw logical inferences. <break time="0.8s" /> But this is the way the story of discovery is told. <break time="0.8s" /> Rather than how it actually happens. <break time="0.8s" /> For this. <break time="0.8s" /> We first need. <break time="0.8s" /> The ability to analyse concepts and, out of them, create new patterns. <break time="0.8s" /> Through which we look at the world. <break time="0.8s" /> And organise our information about it. <break time="0.8s" /> Once we have revealed. <break time="0.8s" /> The pattern of ideas at the heart of our concept. <break time="0.8s" /> We can then manipulate it. <break time="0.8s" /> And form new ones. <break time="0.8s" /> Many of the most significant breakthroughs in our understanding. <break time="0.8s" /> Have come about not because researchers have new or better data. <break time="0.8s" /> But because of the quality of their thinking. <break time="0.8s" /> And the type of concepts they create. <break time="0.8s" /> In many cases. <break time="0.8s" /> When researchers have been faced with stubborn problems that defy solution. <break time="0.8s" /> The answers have only finally come. <break time="0.8s" /> As a result of being able to think. <break time="0.8s" /> Outside the accepted concepts and methods of their disciplines.
